question: Which statement best describes Building (next build)?
options: Vercel (the company behind Next.js) offers zero-config deployment: connect a Git repo and every push builds and deploys automatically. It maps Next features to its platform — static/ISR pages to the CDN, Server Components/SSR and route handlers to serverless functions, and edge-runtime code to the edge network. It's the fastest path and supports preview deployments and on-demand revalidation out of the box.

You can host Next anywhere Node runs: `next build && next start`, or use `output: 'standalone'` so the build emits a minimal server bundle with only required node_modules — ideal for small Docker images. In a container you copy the .next/standalone output and run `node server.js`. Self-hosting gives full control (your cloud, your network) at the cost of managing scaling, caching, and ISR storage yourself.

`next build` compiles your app for production: it bundles and minifies JS, pre-renders static pages (SSG/ISR), and prints a route summary showing which routes are static (○) vs dynamic (ƒ). You then serve it with `next start` (a Node server). The build output is the contract for whatever you deploy onto, so reading its static/dynamic markers tells you exactly how each route will behave in production.

`output: 'export'` renders every page to plain HTML/CSS/JS at build time, producing an `out/` folder you can host on ANY static host or CDN (S3, GitHub Pages, Nginx) with no Node server. The trade-off: you lose server-only features — SSR/dynamic rendering, route handlers, ISR, and Image Optimization (unless you supply a custom loader). It's perfect for fully static marketing/doc sites.

You opt in per route with `export const runtime = 'edge'`. Use edge for light, latency-sensitive/geo logic (middleware, simple handlers) and Node for heavy work or incompatible dependencies.

question: Which statement best describes Edge vs Node runtime?
options: A CDN caches static assets and static/ISR HTML at edge locations near users, so most requests never hit your origin — giving low latency and high scalability. Next's static pages, _next/static assets, and ISR responses are CDN-cacheable; dynamic SSR responses generally aren't (or use short cache headers). On Vercel this is automatic; self-hosting means putting a CDN (CloudFront, Cloudflare) in front of your server.
